note: The alpha ledger as data. One record per tested CLAIM (a measured relationship), not per strategy (a bundle of them). Seeded from docs/ALPHA_LEDGER.md. Records are either MEASURED (an evidence level and controls) or QUEUED (Untested, with an origin and a proposed test). Only ControlTested edges may contribute to a score; Fragile and Falsified are outcomes, not rungs. See docs/LAB_DESIGN.md.

edges.title: Cross-sectional momentum
edges.claim: Rank a universe by trailing return; the top tercile outperforms the bottom over the next month.

scope.notes: 38 names tested. The crypto arm is a null but with 10 names a tercile is 3 names — underpowered rather than disproven.

edges.title: Time-series trend following — the family, not the parameters
edges.claim: A long-only trend filter on a crypto asset beats holding it, and the specific parameter values carry no information.

scope.notes: Crypto is where it earns return. On indices and gold it matches hold's Sharpe with 2-3x smaller drawdowns — crash insurance, not alpha. Long-only FX: nothing.

effect.notes: Vol-targeted BTC Sharpe 1.19 vs 0.80 hold; maxDD 23% vs 83%. ~40% drawdown for the raw version.

edges.title: Asset-class polarity — crypto trends, equities revert
edges.claim: Crypto price series are positively autocorrelated at swing horizons and equity indices negatively; the correct tool family follows from the asset class.

scope.notes: USE AS A FORK, NOT A DIAL. Collinear with market depth at rho 0.96, and the sign reverses INSIDE crypto — the continuous version is mostly depth wearing another name.

correlatesWith.note: both split on asset class; check overlap before stacking

edges.title: Volume carries forward information — in crypto, and reversed in equities
edges.claim: High relative volume precedes positive forward returns in crypto and negative forward returns in equities.

scope.notes: The SIGN is asset-class dependent — this is one edge with two signs, not two edges.

effect.notes: Crypto survives in all three volume buckets with the same sign (p 0.0002-0.009); the equity arm is significantly negative.

edges.title: Mean reversion to the volume POC
edges.claim: Price displaced from the rolling volume point-of-control reverts toward it over about five days in equities.

scope.notes: REVERSES in crypto — there the same displacement continues.

effect.notes: 38 symbols, 348k bars. A known anomaly; the effect is real and tiny.

correlatesWith.note: the equity half is the polarity fork restated on a specific anchor

edges.title: Exit on the entry signal reversed
edges.claim: Closing a position when the entry signal inverts beats a random exit with the same holding-period distribution — in crypto only.

scope.notes: The equity arm is null (0.53x, 0.84x). This is the ONLY exit rule with measured skill; every mechanical exit tested worthless.

edges.title: FOMC pre-announcement drift
edges.claim: US equities drift upward in the days before a scheduled FOMC announcement.

scope.notes: Four US equity vehicles, same offset, same sign, 224 real dates.

effect.notes: DECAYED: three of four vehicles have lost 70%+ of the effect post-2015 and XLF has gone slightly negative.

decay.note: post-2015 subsample retains ~30% of the full-sample effect

edges.title: Buy dips only above the 200-day moving average
edges.claim: A dip-buy entry filtered by price above its 200-day average beats the same entry unfiltered, and beats random entries under the same filter.

effect.unit: R (random entries under the same filter: 0.007R)

correlatesWith.note: same 200MA regime premise — do not count both

edges.title: The Trading Cross z-score rule
edges.claim: Long when the rolling z-score of price crosses above +1, flat when it crosses back below 0.

scope.notes: 10 of 10 crypto assets beat hold; 0 of 3 traditional. What it does is AVOID DRAWDOWN, not time entries.

correlatesWith.note: a trend filter in z-score clothing; heavily overlapping exposure

edges.title: On-chain valuation (MVRV, NVT) times the market
edges.claim: Low MVRV / NVT readings precede outperformance.

effect.notes: Monotone and significant against a naive baseline — and 0.00 ATR (p = 0.9855) against a matched price/SMA baseline on the same rows.

edges.title: COT positioning predicts returns
edges.claim: Commercial/large-spec positioning extremes precede reversals.

edges.title: Crowding from funding and open interest
edges.claim: Crowded positioning (funding plus OI) precedes mean reversion.

edges.title: Macro release days move price
edges.claim: CPI, NFP, PPI and GDP release days carry an exploitable directional edge.

scope.notes: 457/445/455/487 real FRED dates since 1990.

effect.notes: 2 of 20 release-day cells significant where ~3 false positives are expected across 60 tests; both TLT; neither near Bonferroni. CPI shows nothing anywhere.

correlatesWith.note: THE CONTRAST IS THE FINDING: FOMC is a policy ACTION, CPI/NFP are DATA the market spends the interval forecasting — the surprise should move price, not the date

edges.title: Fixed-percentage scale-outs protect gains
edges.claim: Closing a fixed fraction at fixed profit levels improves the return distribution.

effect.notes: Destroys 95-100% of the return. The R-distribution has a fat right tail and capping it removes the only trades that pay.

edges.title: Fixed-length market cycles (Camel / Lucas, 54-66d BTC)
edges.claim: Assets oscillate on a countable cycle of a characteristic length that can be traded.

effect.notes: 200 surrogate series built by shuffling log returns reproduce the cycle length on every asset, landing inside the claimed band. It is a property of the detector, not of the market.

edges.title: Cipher confluence (oscillator + tape + structure)
edges.claim: Requiring three orthogonal Cipher components to agree produces high-conviction entries.

effect.notes: Structure labels tested indistinguishable from random; SR proximity was a 15-bar lookahead. The components are not orthogonal — they are transforms of the same price series.

edges.title: The Hurst exponent classifies assets as trending or mean-reverting
edges.claim: Hurst separates trending assets from mean-reverting ones and can route the strategy choice.

effect.unit: Hurst range across all 17 asset/timeframe combinations (0.57-0.60)

edges.title: Sentiment (Fear & Greed) adds orthogonal information
edges.claim: A sentiment gate on a technical entry improves it.

effect.unit: the gated spec was byte-identical to the ungated one
effect.notes: When the oscillator buys at a cycle bottom at support you are already in extreme fear. Fear & Greed is a lagging echo of price.

edges.title: A confidence model over price features
edges.claim: A gradient-boosted model over price and indicator features ranks setups usefully.

effect.notes: Stable and calibrated, not a coin flip — and below the threshold that justifies building on it. Asset-tuned models were WORSE. What signal exists lives in regime/vol features, not in the indicator signals.

edges.title: Fibonacci retracement levels are respected
edges.claim: Price respects Fibonacci retracement ratios more often than it respects arbitrary levels drawn on the same swings.

scope.notes: BTC across four timeframes, ~355,000 level tests. Levels go live with the same delay a real trader has (a pivot at bar p is only knowable at p+span).

effect.notes: THE NUMBER THAT EXPLAINS THE FOLKLORE: a RANDOM horizontal line is respected 59% of the time. 'Levels hold about 60% of the time' is true of ANY line — it is a property of the measurement geometry, not evidence the level did anything. Fib confluence does show +4.4% for crowded zones, but random lines reproduce 2.6 of those 4.4 points: crowded zones are ranges, and ranges keep ranging.

correlatesWith.note: same failure shape — a confluence effect that a density/random control reproduces

edges.title: A bullish engulfing weekly candle predicts the next week's direction
edges.claim: After a bullish engulfing weekly candle, the following week closes higher more often than it closes lower — and enough more often to justify trading only that direction all week.

scope.notes: THE CHEAPEST TEST IN THE VIDEO: one directional claim, weekly bars, a stated prior, no discretionary inputs. The control is the base rate of up-weeks for the same asset — an asset that closes up 55% of weeks unconditionally makes a 55% conditional hit rate worthless.

effect.notes: Equities -2.31 pts, 11/39 instruments positive, 0/39 significant where ~2 were expected by chance. Crypto +3.21 pts but 5/10 positive and the era split kills it: H1 +10.4, H2 -1.8. The cheap alternative (last week simply closed up) is flat everywhere too, so there is no plain weekly momentum either.

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: if I see that the previous weekly candle is bullish engulfing it's more likely than not that the next week is also going to have more bullishness than bearishness ... is there a chance the next candle is bearish? yes, but it's way lower chance

edges.title: Position size should scale with multi-timeframe agreement
edges.claim: Trades taken when weekly bias, daily structure and the zone all agree have higher expectancy than trades taken when they conflict — enough to justify sizing 6% versus 1%.

scope.notes: THE UNTESTED CORNER. Twenty edges in this registry and not one is about SIZING. The claim is a conditional-expectancy test: bucket trades by how many timeframes agree and compare per-trade R. Watch for the tautology trap — if the bias filter and the entry are derived from the same price series, agreement is partly arithmetic.

effect.notes: Null, and THE OVERLAP CHECK IS THE FINDING: 'close above the 50-bar mean' is true at 100.0% of entries against a 23-30% base rate, because a z-score cross upward mechanically implies it. That condition cannot discriminate between entries, so '3 of 3' is really '2 of 2'. With that understood equities are flat (+0.313/+0.308/+0.349 across buckets) and crypto is non-monotone with the MIDDLE bucket best. Neither survives a random-subset null. FIRST MEASUREMENT THIS LAB HAS MADE ABOUT SIZING. HONEST LIMIT: one entry on daily bars, versus his 5-minute entries under weekly/daily/30m structure.

correlatesWith.note: same shape — a higher-timeframe regime filter conditioning a lower-timeframe entry

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: some of analysis is not just for me to decide if I'm going to buy or sell but it's more like me shaving off risk ... if everything is in structure everything is bullish, beautiful zones, I'm going to risk more; if there's things that doesn't tick the box I'm shaving off my risk

edges.title: How price approaches a level predicts whether the level holds
edges.claim: A level approached by one-way momentum holds less often than one approached in a two-way, alternating fashion; and a level price has ranged around for a long time holds less often than one approached cleanly.

scope.notes: CHEAPEST REAL TEST WE CAN RUN — the respect harness (RespectCommand, LevelRespectAnalyzer) already measures whether a level holds, with surrogate controls. This adds one conditioning variable. Note the internal tension in the source: he shaves risk on one-way momentum INTO the level, yet says he prefers aggressive approaches over price hanging around the level. Both halves are separately measurable.

effect.notes: Every daily bucket is a null; the largest real-vs-random difference is -1.2 pts at p=0.708. Real levels DO hold less after loitering (47.5% -> 42.7%) and random lines do exactly the same, so the conditioning describes the measurement. Baseline: real levels 46.2% vs random lines 46.7% -- real levels are not better than random lines at all, which independently reproduces the fib finding under a different respect definition. A 4h crypto arm shows three of six buckets at p<0.05 with inconsistent signs; recorded, not believed.

correlatesWith.note: MUST reuse that study's control — a random line is respected 59% of the time, so any conditional respect rate is meaningless without the matched random-level arm

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: if it's slowly approaching my supply or demand there's no momentum against me, I'm going to continue to hold full risk ... if the price is just going crazy into my supply and demand, momentum is against me, I'm going to shave off my risk. Also I don't like when the price hangs around my liquidity too long because that ranging is just accumulation of stop losses

edges.claim: Supply/demand levels formed during an instrument's primary sessions (London/New York for EURUSD) are respected more often than levels formed outside them.

scope.notes: Cheap: tag each level by the session it formed in, then compare respect rates — the existing respect harness with one extra column. Confound to control: session also determines volatility and volume, so match on those before claiming the session did anything. Needs an FX intraday source before it can be run.

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: if I'm trading EURUSD I'm only looking for liquidity in London and New York session ... people make a big mistake where they're looking for EURUSD liquidity inside of Asian session

edges.title: Sweep and reclaim: breach equal highs, then close back inside the range
edges.claim: Entering when price breaches a cluster of equal highs/lows and then CLOSES back inside the range beats entering on the breach itself, and beats a random entry at the same moments.

scope.notes: Algorithmically definable, which most of this video's 'liquidity' language is not: equal highs within a tolerance, a breach, a close back inside within N bars. Two controls needed — random entries at the same timestamps, and the same entry WITHOUT the reclaim requirement, which isolates the part he says matters.

effect.notes: Not supported. The one arm resembling the claim -- crypto daily, +0.754 R for waiting -- is the SMALLEST sample (n=241) and is contradicted by both larger ones: on crypto 4h both real arms underperform random entries, and on equities the difference has the wrong sign at a fortieth of the size. Even at face value, almost all of the crypto-daily gap is the breach arm being bad (-0.637 vs a -0.137 random floor) rather than the reclaim being good: waiting avoids a poor entry rather than creating a good one, which is the polarity finding restated -- do not short a crypto breakout.

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: you have series of equal highs, a move up, and then back into the range — that move back into the range is a confirmation of my entry ... I need the closed candle, not the open candle

edges.title: A fixed 1:3 reward-to-risk target maximises accumulated profit
edges.claim: Over many trades a fixed 1:3 target accumulates more profit than 1:1, 1:2 or 1:8 — with a small runner left on beyond it.

scope.notes: DIRECTLY CONTRADICTS our exit finding, which is what makes it worth running. We measured that fixed-percentage scale-outs destroy 95-100% of the return because the R-distribution has a fat right tail — but that was CRYPTO DAILY. His market is intraday FX and indices. The real question underneath is not '1:3 or not' but 'does the fat right tail exist in intraday FX at all?' Measure the R-distribution FIRST, per asset class, then the target choice answers itself. Note he keeps a 10-20% runner at breakeven, which is a hedge against exactly the tail we measured.

effect.notes: Falsified in both classes. Total R rises monotonically 1:1 through 1:8 and letting the signal decide beats every fixed target: crypto +3.265 R/trade vs +0.155 at 1:3, equities +0.321 vs +0.134. The distribution says why before any target is tested -- the median trade LOSES (-0.75R) and the top 10% of trades carry 101% (crypto) and 245% (equities) of total R, so in equities the other 90% collectively lose money. Extends EXIT_FINDINGS: the fat right tail is not a crypto peculiarity. HONEST LIMIT: his market is intraday FX with 15-pip stops and we have no FX data; this shifts the burden rather than settling it.

correlatesWith.note: the crypto arm of this question is already answered and the answer was NO — so run this as an asset-class fork, not as a fresh question

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: I tried my strategy with 1:1, 1:2, 1:8 over hundreds of trades. 1:3 is my ideal ... 1:3 had the best, not the win rate, but best profit when it's accumulated over many trades

edges.title: Stopping after consecutive losses improves results
edges.claim: Stopping for the day after two consecutive losses, and for the week after four, improves outcomes.

scope.notes: Has a clean prior test: if trade outcomes are serially INDEPENDENT the rule cannot change expectancy, only variance — so measure the autocorrelation of trade outcomes first. If it is zero, the rule is behavioural rather than statistical, which is a legitimate reason to keep it and a dishonest reason to claim an edge from it.

effect.notes: No statistical basis: outcomes are serially independent, slightly negative if anything, so a stop-after-N-losses rule cannot move expectancy -- only variance. That makes it a BEHAVIOURAL rule, which is a good reason to keep it and a dishonest reason to claim an edge from it.

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: if I have two losses in a row I'm done for the day, and if I have four losses in a row I'm done for the week

edges.title: A 0-1 'risk metric' from price extension over its own history
edges.claim: A composite normalised to 0-1 from price relative to its long-term moving averages, rank-scaled over the asset's own history, identifies high-risk and low-risk zones better than the plain price-over-SMA distance it is built from.

scope.notes: Benjamin Cowen's rainbow risk metric, as a general construction rather than his exact undisclosed formula. THREE TRAPS TO BUILD AROUND, all of which this project has already been bitten by. (1) LOOKAHEAD: normalising over the FULL history uses the future to rank the past — every published rainbow chart does this. Must be an EXPANDING-WINDOW percentile using only prior data, which is what makes the honest version look far worse than the picture. (2) THE BASELINE: the metric IS a price/SMA transform, so the only meaningful test is whether the composite beats its own simplest component — the exact control that killed MVRV (matched price/SMA baseline gave p = 0.9855 where the raw signal gave 0.0002). (3) SAMPLE SIZE: on BTC the whole claim rests on three cycles, and a diminishing-returns correction fitted to those same three cycles is retrospective selection, not evidence.

effect.notes: THE LOOKAHEAD PREMIUM IS 2.3x: ranking against the whole series (what a published rainbow chart shows) gives a 6.9-point spread in crypto; ranking against prior data only, which is all a trader can do, gives 3.0. More than half the picture's apparent power comes from knowing the future. The 0-1 normalisation then adds almost nothing over its own raw input (3.0 vs 2.6 for plain log price/MA) -- the same control that killed the on-chain metrics, landing the same way. Equities are a null with the WRONG SIGN (-0.8 pts, high-risk decile has higher forward returns, 2 of 9 steps monotone), which is the asset-class polarity finding reappearing. What remains is a weak crypto signal that is mostly 'price is far above its 200-day average', across three cycles.

correlatesWith.note: same shape and probably the same fate — a normalised valuation band that must be run against a matched price/SMA baseline on the same rows
built from the same price-over-long-MA information

origin.quote: PARAPHRASE, no transcript captured: a 0-1 risk value per asset, rendered as rainbow bands, built from price relative to long-term moving averages and normalised over the asset's history with a diminishing-returns correction for later cycles.

edges.title: A bearish engulfing weekly candle precedes a down week in crypto
edges.claim: In crypto, the week after a bearish engulfing weekly candle closes down more often than that asset's unconditional down-week rate.

scope.notes: FOUND WHILE TESTING THE OPPOSITE. The bullish claim from the video is dead; its mirror was free to test and is the only arm that survived anything. Consistent with this project's repeated finding that crypto's two directions are not mirrors of each other.

effect.notes: Cheap-alternative control (plain down week) is +0.04 pts, so the structure is doing the work and not momentum. Era split holds and strengthens: H1 +5.2, H2 +12.0. THREE REASONS IT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: four pooled tests were run so the Bonferroni threshold is 0.0125 and 0.013 sits just outside; the ten crypto instruments are not ten independent samples because they move together, which narrows the pooled null dishonestly; and 209 signals is a small base.

correlatesWith.note: the same study; this is the mirror arm of the falsified claim

edges.title: The surprise moves price, not the scheduled date
edges.claim: Post-earnings returns scale with the earnings SURPRISE (actual minus consensus EPS), even though the release DATE itself carries no directional edge.

scope.notes: THE FOLLOW-UP THE MACRO STUDY EARNED. Release dates for CPI/NFP/PPI/GDP tested null while FOMC did not, and the proposed explanation was that FOMC is a policy ACTION while CPI/NFP are DATA the market spends the interval forecasting -- so the surprise should move price rather than the date. That was untestable while macro consensus was paywalled. It is testable on EARNINGS: Alpha Vantage's free EARNINGS endpoint carries reportedEPS, estimatedEPS and surprise back to 1996 (verified 2026-08-01). Controls needed: post-earnings drift is a documented anomaly, so the arm that matters is whether surprise MAGNITUDE ranks forward returns beyond the plain event-date effect, plus an exposure-matched null on the drift window.

correlatesWith.note: this is the surprise-side test of the same hypothesis that the date-side test falsified
the action-versus-data distinction these two together are meant to settle

origin.quote: PARAPHRASE of our own MACRO_EVENT_FINDINGS conclusion: FOMC is a policy action and CPI/NFP are data the market spends the interval forecasting, so the surprise should move price, not the date.
